o: They derive from the sclerotome parts of the somites

Vertebrae develop from the sclerotome (medial) parts of the somites of the paraxial mesoderm.
The sclerotome cells migrate around the notochord and neural tube. (Last's p. 557-8)
Each vertebra forms from adjacent caudal and cranial halves of two somites

Each vertebra forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome and the cranial half of the next, so vertebrae lie in intersegmental planes.
That is why the segmental nerves and arteries pass between vertebrae. (Last's p. 557-8)
Each cartilaginous ring ossifies from a single centre

Each cartilaginous vertebral ring ossifies from three primary centres: one for the centrum and one for each half of the neural arch.
Not a single centre. (Last's p. 557-8)
Failure of one half of the double centrum centre causes spina bifida

Failure of one half of the (double) centrum centre causes a hemivertebra, producing congenital scoliosis. Spina bifida results from failure of the neural arch halves to fuse.
Different centres, different defects. (Last's p. 557-8)
All vertebrae ossify in hyaline cartilage

All vertebrae are preformed in hyaline cartilage and ossify from three primary centres.
Unlike the vault of the skull, which ossifies in membrane. (Last's p. 557-8)
The laminae are completely united by 2 years

The two halves of the neural arch begin uniting after birth and are fully joined by about 2 years.
Failure gives spina bifida occulta. (Last's p. 557-8)
The neurocentral junctions are united by about 2 years

The neurocentral junctions (between arch and centrum) unite by about 7 years, not 2.
A neurocentral line seen on X-ray in a young child is normal. (Last's p. 557-8)
The ring epiphyses fuse with the body around puberty

The ring epiphyses appear soon after puberty and fuse with the body in the early twenties.
They are not fused at puberty. (Last's p. 557-8)
The bifid cervical spines have double secondary centres

The bifid cervical spines have a double secondary centre, one for each tip.
Secondary centres appear after puberty. (Last's p. 557-8)
Mamillary processes of T12 and lumbar vertebrae have secondary centres

The mammillary processes of T12 and the lumbar vertebrae have their own secondary centres after puberty.
So do the transverse processes and spines. (Last's p. 557-8)
Cervical and lumbar costal elements have separate bony centres

Cervical and lumbar costal elements ossify from the neural arch, without separate centres. An occasional separate centre gives a cervical or lumbar rib.
Separate centres are abnormal here. (Last's p. 557-8)
Sacral costal elements have no separate centres

The sacral costal elements do have separate centres, appearing at about 6 months of fetal life.
They form the lateral parts of the sacrum. (Last's p. 557-8)

questions.s: Ossification of the atlas and axis (Last's):
o: The atlas lateral masses ossify at the seventh week

The atlas ossifies from a centre in each lateral mass, appearing at the seventh week.
These two centres extend into the posterior arch. (Last's p. 557-8)
The anterior arch centre appears at the first year

A centre for the anterior arch appears at about one year and fuses with the lateral masses at about 7 years.
Before then the anterior arch is cartilaginous. (Last's p. 557-8)
The posterior arch of the atlas unites at 12 years

The two halves of the posterior arch of the atlas unite at about the fourth year, not 12.
Failure leaves a posterior cleft. (Last's p. 557-8)
The tip of the dens fuses at 3 years

The centre for the tip of the dens appears at about 3 years and fuses at about 12.
So the tip is separate for many years (os terminale if it fails to fuse). (Last's p. 557-8)
The dens has two half-side centres appearing at the fifth month

The dens has two half-side centres appearing at the fifth fetal month, which fuse about two months later.
Hence the dens may appear bifid on rare occasions. (Last's p. 557-8)
The dens unites with the body at 3 years

The dens and the body of the axis unite at about 3 years.
Before that, the synchondrosis can be mistaken for a fracture. (Last's p. 557-8)
The lower ring epiphysis fuses at about 12 years

The lower ring epiphysis of the axis body fuses at about 25 years, not 12.
Ring epiphyses fuse late. (Last's p. 557-8)
The anterior arch epiphyses of the atlas fuse at 3 years

The anterior arch epiphyses of the atlas fuse at about 7 years, not 3.
The dens base fuses at 3. (Last's p. 557-8)
The primary curvature is retained in the thoracic and sacral regions

The primary (fetal) curvature, concave forward, is retained in the thoracic and sacral regions. The cervical and lumbar curves are secondary.
They appear with head-holding and walking. (Last's p. 535-6)
The costal facets of thoracic vertebrae lie on the neural arch, not the centrum

The costal facets of thoracic vertebrae lie on the neural arch, not the centrum, because the neurocentral junction lies in front of them.
A Last's morphological point. (Last's p. 535-6)
Lumbar transverse processes are true transverse elements

Lumbar transverse processes are costal elements. The mammillary process and accessory tubercle are the true transverse elements.
So the "transverse process" of a lumbar vertebra is really a rib element. (Last's p. 535-6)
A lumbar rib results from fusion of the costal element

A lumbar rib results from failure of the costal element to fuse with the vertebra, not from fusion.
The same applies to a cervical rib. (Last's p. 535-6)
It is a secondary cartilaginous joint

The intervertebral disc is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis).
Hyaline cartilage plates are joined by fibrocartilage. (Last's p. 537)
The nucleus pulposus lies posteriorly in the adult disc

In the adult disc the nucleus pulposus lies nearer the back, because the notochord moved backward during development.
That is one reason herniations go backward. (Last's p. 537)
The nucleus pulposus is about 50% of the disc

Last's says the nucleus pulposus is about 15 percent of the disc, not 50 percent.
The annulus makes up most of the disc. (Last's p. 537)
The nucleus pulposus is about 70% water at birth

The nucleus pulposus is about 90 percent water at birth, falling to about 70 percent in old age.
Loss of water explains loss of height with age. (Last's p. 537)
The anterior longitudinal ligament broadens as it passes down

The anterior longitudinal ligament widens as it descends to the sacrum.
It resists extension. (Last's p. 537)
The posterior longitudinal ligament is firmly attached over the discs

The posterior longitudinal ligament is firmly attached over the discs and loosely over the bodies.
Basivertebral veins emerge under it. (Last's p. 537)
The posterior longitudinal ligament broadens as it descends

The posterior longitudinal ligament narrows as it descends, which leaves the lumbar discs less protected posterolaterally.
Contrast the anterior ligament, which widens. (Last's p. 537)
The anterior longitudinal ligament begins at the body of the axis

The anterior longitudinal ligament begins at the anterior tubercle of the atlas; the posterior longitudinal ligament begins at the axis (continuing up as the tectorial membrane).
Different upper ends. (Last's p. 537)
It extended as far cranially as the sella turcica

The notochord extended cranially as far as the sella turcica.
Chordomas can therefore arise in the clivus as well as the sacrum. (Last's p. 537)
The apical ligament of the dens is a notochordal remnant

The apical ligament of the dens, running to the foramen magnum, is a notochordal remnant, like the nucleus pulposus.
It is weak and functionally unimportant. (Last's p. 537)
Its remnant in the disc is the annulus fibrosus

The notochordal remnant in the disc is the nucleus pulposus, not the annulus fibrosus.
The annulus comes from sclerotome. (Last's p. 537)
The alar ligaments are notochordal remnants

Only the apical ligament is a notochordal remnant; the alar ligaments are not.
The alar ligaments are strong check ligaments. (Last's p. 537)
An L5/S1 disc prolapse usually irritates the S1 root

A posterolateral L5/S1 disc prolapse misses the L5 root, which has already exited higher in its foramen, and compresses the S1 root.
The ankle jerk is then reduced. (Last's p. 539)
A C6/7 disc irritates the C7 root

In the cervical spine each root exits above its vertebra, so a C6/7 disc affects the C7 root.
Triceps weakness and reflex loss result. (Last's p. 539)
An L4/5 disc prolapse usually irritates the L4 root

An L4/5 disc prolapse usually irritates the L5 root (the one below).
The L4 root has already left above the disc. (Last's p. 539)
Uncovertebral joints are synovial

Last's says the uncovertebral joints are degenerative clefts, not true synovial joints.
They can still cause foraminal narrowing. (Last's p. 539)
Facet joints are supplied from their own level and the level above

The facet joints are supplied from the medial branch of the dorsal ramus at their own level and the level above; each nerve supplies two joints.
So two levels must be blocked to denervate one joint. (Last's p. 539)
Ligamenta flava attach to the front of the upper lamina and back of the lower

Each ligamentum flavum runs from the front of the lamina above to the back of the lamina below.
It is yellow elastic tissue. (Last's p. 539)
Ligamenta flava are relaxed by flexion

The ligamenta flava are stretched by flexion, not relaxed.
Their elasticity helps return the spine to upright. (Last's p. 539)
The supraspinous ligament continues in the neck as the anterior longitudinal ligament

In the neck the supraspinous ligament continues as the ligamentum nuchae.
The anterior longitudinal ligament lies on the front of the bodies. (Last's p. 539)

questions.s: The vertebral canal and intervertebral foramina (Last's):
o: The canal becomes progressively smaller from above down

The vertebral canal becomes progressively smaller from above down.
It is largest in the cervical and upper lumbar regions relative to the cord. (Last's p. 540)
Pedicles form the upper and lower boundaries of each foramen

The pedicles form the upper and lower boundaries of each intervertebral foramen.
The disc and bodies lie in front and the facet joint behind. (Last's p. 540)
In the cervical spine only the body above bounds the foramen anteriorly

In the cervical spine the intervertebral foramen is bounded anteriorly by parts of both the body above and the body below (with the disc and uncovertebral region).
So not only the body above. (Last's p. 540)
The lumbar spine permits free rotation

The lumbar spine permits almost no rotation, because of the sagittal orientation of its facet joints.
Rotation occurs mainly in the thoracic spine. (Last's p. 540)
Thoracic rotation occurs mainly above T9

Thoracic rotation occurs mainly above T9; the lower three or four thoracic vertebrae, with more lumbar-type facets, do not rotate.
Most trunk rotation is upper thoracic. (Last's p. 540)
The atlantoaxial joints allow rotation only

The atlanto-axial joints allow rotation; flexion and extension occur at the atlanto-occipital joints.
About half of all neck rotation occurs at C1/2. (Last's p. 540)
The atlanto-occipital joints allow rotation

The atlanto-occipital joints allow flexion, extension and some lateral flexion, but no rotation.
Rotation is at the atlanto-axial joints. (Last's p. 540)
Cervical facets lie on the circumference of a circle centred on the body

The thoracic facets lie on the circumference of a circle centred on the vertebral body, which permits rotation. Cervical facets do not.
That is why thoracic rotation is possible. (Last's p. 540)
The anterior arch is the ossified hypochordal bow

The anterior arch of the atlas is the ossified hypochordal bow, homologous with the central band of the radiate ligament of the ribs.
A Last's morphological point. (Last's p. 541-2)
C1 and C2 anterior rami pass behind the atlantal joints

The atlantal facets lie in line with the uncovertebral joints, so the C1 and C2 anterior rami pass behind them.
Lower cervical rami pass behind the uncovertebral region too. (Last's p. 541-2)
The inferior facet of the atlas is kidney-shaped

The superior facet of the atlas is kidney-shaped (for the occipital condyle); the inferior facet is round and flat.
The superior facet is concave. (Last's p. 541-2)
Rectus capitis posterior major attaches to the posterior arch of the atlas

Rectus capitis posterior minor is the only muscle attached to the posterior arch of the atlas (at its tubercle). Rectus capitis posterior major attaches to the axis spine.
Minor on the atlas, major on the axis. (Last's p. 541-2)
The dens bears no weight

The dens bears no weight; weight passes from the atlas through the superior articular facets of the axis.
The dens acts as a pivot. (Last's p. 541-2)
Its foramen transversarium is directed upwards and outwards

The foramen transversarium of the axis is directed upward and outward, giving the vertebral artery a lateral bend.
The artery then turns medially above the atlas. (Last's p. 541-2)
The dens is the centrum of the atlas

Last's says the dens is not the centrum of the atlas. Note that most embryology texts describe the dens as derived largely from the atlas centrum, so expect this point to be contested.
Answer according to Last's. (Last's p. 541-2)
Semispinalis capitis inserts into the bifid spine of the axis

Semispinalis cervicis inserts into the bifid spine of the axis. Semispinalis capitis inserts into the occipital bone.
Capitis goes to the head. (Last's p. 541-2)
The tectorial membrane is continuous with the PLL

The tectorial membrane is the upward continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament from the axis to the foramen magnum.
It covers the dens from behind. (Last's p. 541-2)
The alar ligaments limit rotation

The strong alar ligaments, from the dens to the occipital condyles, limit rotation of the head.
They are check ligaments. (Last's p. 541-2)
The tectorial membrane lies behind the dura

The tectorial membrane lies in front of the dura, firmly attached to it, not behind it.
It is the most posterior ligament, just in front of the dura. (Last's p. 541-2)
The apical ligament lies behind the cruciform ligament

The apical ligament lies in front of the upper longitudinal band of the cruciform ligament, not behind it.
From front to back: apical, cruciform, tectorial membrane. (Last's p. 541-2)
They are supplied by C1

Both atlanto-occipital membranes are supplied by C1.
The joint and its membranes share a nerve supply. (Last's p. 541-2)
The posterior membrane is deficient laterally for the vertebral artery and C1

The posterior atlanto-occipital membrane is deficient at each end for the vertebral artery and C1 nerve.
These pass beneath its lateral free border. (Last's p. 541-2)
The anterior membrane attaches to the posterior border of the anterior arch

The anterior atlanto-occipital membrane attaches to the anterior (upper) border of the anterior arch of the atlas.
It continues the anterior longitudinal ligament. (Last's p. 541-2)
The lateral atlantoaxial joints are supplied by C1

The lateral atlanto-axial joints are supplied by C2, not C1.
The C2 nerve lies just behind them. (Last's p. 541-2)
Rotatores occur only in the thoracic spine

Rotatores (from a transverse process to the root of the spine above) are found only in the thoracic spine.
They are the deepest transversospinalis muscles. (Last's p. 544)
Semispinalis capitis is the chief extensor of the head

Semispinalis capitis, from upper thoracic and lower cervical transverse processes to the occiput, is the chief extensor of the head.
It is a thick muscle under trapezius. (Last's p. 544)
Multifidus extends from the sacrum to C1

Multifidus extends from the sacrum to C2, not C1.
C1 has no spine for it to reach. (Last's p. 544)
Iliocostalis forms the most medial part of erector spinae

Iliocostalis forms the most lateral part of erector spinae; spinalis is the most medial.
Longissimus is intermediate. (Last's p. 544)
Splenius cervicis attaches to the transverse processes of C1-3 or C1-4

Splenius cervicis inserts into the transverse processes of C1 to C3 or C1 to C4, deep to levator scapulae.
Splenius capitis inserts into the mastoid and superior nuchal line. (Last's p. 544)
Longus colli and psoas belong to the flexor group

Longus colli and psoas belong to the vertebral flexor group, supplied by anterior rami.
They lie in front of the transverse processes. (Last's p. 544)
Splenius is supplied by the accessory nerve

Splenius is supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami, as an intrinsic back muscle, not by the accessory nerve.
The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. (Last's p. 544)
The vertebral flexors derive from the outer layer of the body wall

Last's says the vertebral flexors derive from the innermost layer of the body wall, not the outer layer.
They correspond to transversus abdominis in layer. (Last's p. 544)
Its floor is the posterior arch of the atlas and posterior atlanto-occipital membrane

The floor of the suboccipital triangle is the posterior arch of the atlas and the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane.
The vertebral artery lies on the arch. (Last's p. 546)
The suboccipital nerve and vertebral artery cross its floor

The vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve (C1) lie on the floor of the triangle.
The nerve emerges between the artery and the arch. (Last's p. 546)
It is bounded by rectus capitis posterior minor

The triangle is bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and the two oblique muscles. Rectus minor lies medial to it.
Minor does not form a side. (Last's p. 546)
The greater occipital nerve crosses its floor

The greater occipital nerve crosses the roof of the triangle, not its floor.
It winds around the lower border of obliquus inferior. (Last's p. 546)
They are supplied by the posterior ramus of C1

The suboccipital recti and obliques are supplied by the posterior ramus of C1 (the suboccipital nerve).
It has no cutaneous branch. (Last's p. 546)
Inferior oblique runs from the axis spine to the atlas lateral mass

Inferior oblique runs from the spine of the axis to the transverse process (lateral mass) of the atlas. It rotates the atlas.
Despite its name it does not reach the skull. (Last's p. 546)
Superior oblique runs from the axis spine to the occiput

Superior oblique runs from the transverse process (lateral mass) of the atlas to the occiput, not from the axis spine.
The axis spine gives origin to the inferior oblique and rectus major. (Last's p. 546)
The suboccipital nerve supplies skin of the occiput

The suboccipital nerve has no cutaneous branch; neither of its rami supplies skin.
The occipital skin is C2 (greater occipital). (Last's p. 546)

questions.s: The vertebral artery in the neck (Last's):
o: It enters the C6 foramen transversarium

The vertebral artery usually enters the foramen transversarium of C6, not C7.
About 5 percent enter at another level. (Last's p. 547-8)
It passes behind the atlanto-occipital joint

Above the atlas the vertebral artery turns medially behind the atlanto-occipital joint, grooving the posterior arch.
This is its suboccipital part. (Last's p. 547-8)
It runs behind the emerging cervical nerves

The vertebral artery runs in front of the emerging cervical nerves, not behind them.
The nerves pass behind it in the transverse processes. (Last's p. 547-8)
Vertebral veins accompany it inside the skull

Last's says the vertebral veins exist only in the neck; they do not accompany the artery inside the skull.
No veins accompany the vertebral and basilar arteries intracranially. (Last's p. 547-8)
One emerges with the artery through C6

One vertebral vein emerges with the artery from the C6 foramen transversarium.
It forms from a plexus around the artery. (Last's p. 547-8)
One passes alone through C7 foramen transversarium

A second vertebral vein passes alone through the C7 foramen transversarium.
That foramen does not carry the artery. (Last's p. 547-8)
They drain into the internal jugular vein

The vertebral veins drain into the brachiocephalic vein, not the internal jugular vein.
They enter its back at the root of the neck. (Last's p. 547-8)
The C7 foramen transmits the vertebral artery

The C7 foramen does not transmit the vertebral artery, which enters at C6.
It carries only a vein and a grey ramus. (Last's p. 547-8)
It grooves the occipitomastoid suture deep to digastric

The occipital artery grooves the occipitomastoid suture deep to the posterior belly of digastric and longissimus capitis.
It runs back to the scalp. (Last's p. 547-8)
The hypoglossal nerve hooks round it from behind

XII hooks round the occipital artery from behind, held down by its lower sternocleidomastoid branch.
A landmark for finding XII. (Last's p. 547-8)
It crosses the floor of the suboccipital triangle

The occipital artery crosses the upper part of the roof of the suboccipital triangle, not its floor.
The vertebral artery is on the floor. (Last's p. 547-8)
Its upper sternocleidomastoid branch is a guide to the facial nerve

The upper sternocleidomastoid branch of the occipital artery is a guide to the accessory nerve, not the facial nerve.
The lower branch relates to XII. (Last's p. 547-8)
The spines are steepest at T7

The spines of the thoracic vertebrae are steepest (most downward-sloping) at T7, then level out towards T12.
So the T7 spine overlies the T8 body. (Last's p. 548-50)
The upper six costotransverse facets are concave

The upper six costotransverse facets are concave (allowing rotation of the rib); the lower ones are flat (allowing gliding).
This difference affects rib movement. (Last's p. 548-50)
The superior articular facets face anteromedially

The superior articular facets of thoracic vertebrae face posterolaterally, not anteromedially.
They lie on the arc of a circle, allowing rotation. (Last's p. 548-50)
The body takes part in the boundary of the foramen above

In thoracic vertebrae the pedicle is flush with the top of the body, so the body does not take part in the boundary of the foramen above.
The disc and body below bound it. (Last's p. 548-50)
T1 has a whole facet for the first rib

T1 has a complete round facet for the head of the first rib and a demifacet below for the second.
It is transitional. (Last's p. 548-50)
T12 has a lumbar-type inferior facet

The inferior articular processes of T12 are lumbar in type, facing laterally.
So rotation is limited below it. (Last's p. 548-50)
T1 pedicles are flush with the top of the body

The pedicles of T1 attach below the upper margin of the body, as in cervical vertebrae, not flush with the top.
T1 is transitional. (Last's p. 548-50)
The T12 posterior ramus runs between its mamillary and accessory processes

Last's says it is the T11 posterior ramus that runs between the mammillary and accessory processes of T12.
A small Last's detail. (Last's p. 548-50)
L5 is the only vertebra whose transverse process joins the body

Only L5 has a transverse process that joins the body as well as the pedicle; it is short and massive.
It bears weight transmitted through the iliolumbar ligament. (Last's p. 550-2)
The lumbar lordosis is mainly due to wedge-shaped discs

Last's says the lumbar lordosis is produced mainly by wedge-shaped discs.
Rather than wedge-shaped vertebral bodies. (Last's p. 550-2)
L1 usually has the longest transverse process

The longest lumbar transverse process is usually L3 or L4 (Last's says L4); L1 is not the longest. L5 is short and massive.
The transverse processes of L1 are shortest. (Last's p. 550-2)
Lumbar bodies are heart-shaped

Lumbar vertebral bodies are kidney-shaped, not heart-shaped.
Thoracic bodies are heart-shaped. (Last's p. 550-2)
Psoas spans the vertebral concavity on fibrous arches

Psoas spans the concavity at the sides of the lumbar bodies on fibrous arches. The lumbar vessels and sympathetic rami pass beneath them.
This protects the vessels. (Last's p. 550-2)
The arcuate ligaments attach to the L1 transverse process

The medial and lateral arcuate ligaments attach to the transverse process of L1.
The diaphragm arises from them. (Last's p. 550-2)
Quadratus lumborum lies medial to the ridge on the transverse process

Quadratus lumborum lies lateral to the ridge on the transverse process; psoas is medial.
The ridge marks the attachment of the anterior layer of the thoracolumbar fascia. (Last's p. 550-2)
The L5 inferior facets face backwards

The inferior facets of L5 face forward, fitting into the backward-facing superior facets of the sacrum.
This prevents L5 sliding forward. (Last's p. 550-2)
The sacroiliac joint itself is not weight-bearing

Last's says the sacroiliac joint itself is not weight-bearing; the strong interosseous and posterior ligaments bear the weight.
The sacrum hangs from the ligaments. (Last's p. 552-4)
Medial borders of the anterior foramina are vertebral bodies

The medial borders of the anterior sacral foramina are formed by the fused vertebral bodies; the rest of the lateral mass is costal in origin.
The costal elements form the alae. (Last's p. 552-4)
The sacral hiatus is due to failure of fusion of S1 laminae

The sacral hiatus is due to failure of fusion of the laminae of S5 (and sometimes S4), not S1.
Failure at S1 is spina bifida occulta of S1, which is common but different. (Last's p. 552-4)
The sacral plexus lies medial to the anterior foramina

The sacral plexus lies lateral to the anterior sacral foramina, on piriformis.
The sympathetic trunk lies medial to them. (Last's p. 552-4)
The sympathetic trunk crosses medial to the sacral foramina

The sacral sympathetic trunk runs down medial to the anterior sacral foramina; the sacral plexus is lateral.
The two trunks join in front of the coccyx (ganglion impar). (Last's p. 552-4)
The obturator nerve is the most lateral structure crossing the ala

Crossing the sacral ala from medial to lateral are the sympathetic trunk, the lumbosacral trunk, the iliolumbar artery and the obturator nerve. The obturator nerve is the most lateral.
These structures can be injured in sacral fractures. (Last's p. 552-4)
Sacrotuberous ligament arises above the auricular surface

The sacrotuberous ligament arises below the auricular surface, not above it.
It runs from the back of the sacrum and ilium to the ischial tuberosity. (Last's p. 552-4)
The dural sac in the sacral canal ends at S4

The dural sac in the sacral canal ends at S2, not S4.
Below that the canal contains roots in their own sheaths and the filum. (Last's p. 552-4)
The lateral sacrococcygeal ligament completes the foramen for S5

The lateral sacrococcygeal ligament completes the foramen for the S5 nerve.
It runs between the coccyx and the sacrum. (Last's p. 552-4)
Its tip gives attachment to the anococcygeal raphe

The tip of the coccyx gives attachment to the anococcygeal raphe and part of the external anal sphincter.
Levator ani also attaches nearby. (Last's p. 552-4)
It usually has six pieces

The coccyx usually has four pieces, not six.
The number varies from three to five. (Last's p. 552-4)
Its lower surface lies in the pelvic floor

The upper surface of the coccyx lies in the pelvic floor; the lower surface lies in the buttock.
Coccygeus and levator ani attach to its margins. (Last's p. 552-4)
The C6 anterior tubercle is the carotid tubercle

The large anterior tubercle of C6 is the carotid (Chassaignac's) tubercle, against which the carotid can be compressed.
It is also a stellate block landmark. (Last's p. 555-6)
The posterior root ganglia lie on the lamella behind the foramen

Cervical posterior root ganglia lie on the intertubercular lamella behind the vertebral artery.
They sit in the gutter of the transverse process. (Last's p. 555-6)
Scalenus anterior attaches to posterior tubercles

Scalenus anterior attaches to the anterior tubercles of C3 to C6, not the posterior tubercles.
Scalenus medius and posterior attach to the posterior tubercles. (Last's p. 555-6)
The vertebral body is larger than the vertebral foramen

In typical cervical vertebrae the body is the same size as or smaller than the large triangular vertebral foramen.
The canal is roomy for the cervical enlargement. (Last's p. 555-6)
Its foramen transversarium does not transmit the vertebral artery

The foramen transversarium of C7 usually carries only a vertebral vein and a grey ramus, not the vertebral artery.
The artery enters at C6. (Last's p. 555-6)
Its spine ends in a rounded tubercle, not bifid

C7 (vertebra prominens) has a long spine ending in a single rounded tubercle, not bifid.
It is the first easily palpable spine. (Last's p. 555-6)
Its anterior tubercle is large

The anterior tubercle of C7 is small, giving attachment to scalenus pleuralis and the suprapleural membrane.
C6 has the large one. (Last's p. 555-6)
Its foramen transmits the grey ramus to C8

Last's says the grey ramus through the C7 foramen goes to the C7 anterior ramus, not C8.
Small details are often tested. (Last's p. 555-6)
It has five primary centres

Last's says the axis has five primary centres: the lower body, two half-arches with the lateral parts, and two for the dens and upper body.
More than a typical vertebra. (Last's p. 555-6)
It has seven centres in total

In total the axis has seven centres: five primary, plus the tip of the dens and the lower ring epiphysis.
Secondary centres appear later. (Last's p. 555-6)
The tip of the dens centre appears at 12

The centre for the tip of the dens appears at about 3 years and fuses at about 12.
So 12 is the fusion age, not the appearance. (Last's p. 555-6)
The arch centres appear at the fifth month

The neural arch centres of the axis appear at about the seventh fetal week, not the fifth month.
The dens centres appear at the fifth month. (Last's p. 555-6)

questions.s: Blood supply of the vertebral column (Last's):
o: The deep cervical artery supplies the cervical extensors

The deep cervical artery, with the transverse cervical artery, supplies the cervical extensor muscles.
The deep cervical comes from the costocervical trunk. (Last's p. 555-6)
Vertebral veins communicate with the left renal vein

Through segmental veins the vertebral venous plexuses communicate with the left renal vein, a route for the spread of cancer.
Batson's plexus links many systems. (Last's p. 555-6)
Basivertebral veins drain into the external vertebral plexus

The basivertebral veins drain into the internal vertebral plexus, not the external.
They emerge from the backs of the bodies into the canal. (Last's p. 555-6)
The external vertebral plexus lies within the vertebral canal

The external vertebral plexus lies outside the canal, around the vertebrae and within the back muscles; the internal plexus lies within the canal.
Their names describe their positions. (Last's p. 555-6)
